title: What's the weather like? — sentences with no subject
goal: Talk about the weather and the seasons, and compare two things — while discovering one of the rare spots where Slovenian is simpler than English: weather sentences have no subject at all.
bekal: describing conditions with the neuter form: *toplo je*, *hladno je*, *oblačno je*
comparing with *-ejši* and *kot*: *topleje kot včeraj*, *najlepši dan*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kdo dežuje?
dialogs.intro: A rainy morning at the dorm window. Budi looks outside and discovers a sentence with no subject.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kot v indonezijščini: hujan. Ena beseda.
lines.literal: like in Indonesian: hujan. one word.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Jutri bo topleje. Menda celo sonce.
lines.id: Tomorrow it'll be warmer. Maybe even sunny, they say.
lines.literal: tomorrow will-be warmer. apparently even sun.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Potem gremo v hribe, če bo lepo.
lines.id: Then let's go to the mountains if it's nice.
lines.literal: then we-go to mountain-pl, if will-be nice.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Velja. Vzemi jakno — vreme se hitro spremeni.
lines.id: Deal. Take a jacket — the weather changes fast here.
lines.literal: it-holds. take-imp jacket-acc — weather self quickly changes.

notes: **Dežuje has no subject, and that's on purpose.** English has to invent a dummy subject — *it is raining*, and nobody knows who "it" is. Slovenian doesn't bother: the verb stands alone, like "hujan" in Indonesian, as Budi points out. One less word to worry about.

**If it's not a verb, use the neuter form.** *Toplo je*, *Hladno je*, *Oblačno je*, *Megleno je*. The form ending in *-o* is the neuter adjective, and it's the fallback whenever there's no noun to agree with. You've already met this pattern in unit 4 with *Zunaj je hrupno*.

**Topleje is an adverb, toplejši is an adjective.** *Jutri bo toplej**e*** (tomorrow it'll be warmer — about conditions), but *toplej**ši** dan* (a warmer day — about a thing). The same split applies across the board: *bolje* versus *boljši*, *lepše* versus *lepši*.

**Menda = apparently, supposedly.** One word for something you've heard but haven't confirmed. Its relatives: *baje* (reportedly), *očitno* (evidently), *verjetno* (probably). All four are very common and very easy — none of them changes form.

**Vreme se hitro spremeni** isn't small talk. Slovenia is smaller than New Jersey, yet it holds the Alps, the Pannonian plain and the Mediterranean coast all at once; rain can move from one to another within an hour. The weather forecast is called **vremenska napoved**, and Slovenians check it as seriously as commuters check traffic.

grammars.title: Vreme — verbs and states with no subject
body: Two groups, and neither needs a single noun in front.
after: The past tense uses the neuter: *Deževalo je* (it was raining), *Toplo je bilo* (it was warm), *Snežilo je* (it was snowing). So does the future: *Jutri bo deževalo*, *Jutri bo toplo*.

To ask: *Kakšno je vreme?* (what's the weather like) or *Kako je zunaj?* (what's it like outside). The most common answers: *Lepo je* (it's nice), *Grdo je* (it's ugly) — and yes, Slovenians really do call bad weather "ugly".

grammars.title: Comparing — more and most
body: To make an adjective "more", add **-ejši** or **-ji**. To make it "most", add the prefix **naj-** in front of that form. Two steps, and the whole comparison system is done.
after: To say "more … than", use **kot**: *Danes je topleje **kot** včeraj* (it's warmer today than yesterday), *Ljubljana je manjša **kot** Jakarta*. *Kot* also means "like" or "as": *bel kot sneg* (white as snow).

If the adjective is long or awkward, Slovenian takes a shortcut with **bolj** (more) and **manj** (less): *bolj zanimiv* (more interesting), *manj drag* (less expensive). This always works, so it's a good backup when the ending form won't come to mind.

blocks.text: Slovenia has four sharply different seasons, and the weather is the number-one conversation opener — much as it is in Britain.
Notice *pet stopinj* — the genitive plural of *stopinja*, because the number is five. The rule from unit 5 turns up again, in the least expected place. For two degrees: *dve stopinji*.

Numbers to prepare yourself for: in January Ljubljana often sits around **zero to minus five** (°C), and the sun sets at 4:00 p.m. In July, by contrast, it can reach thirty-five degrees with dry air — a heat that feels very different from tropical heat.
Four seasons, four adverbs, and four sets of activities. Notice that *spomladi*, *poleti*, *jeseni*, *pozimi* stand on their own, with no preposition.

Two activities in the last column deserve attention, because both are part of Slovenian identity. **Nabiranje gob** — picking mushrooms in the forest in autumn — is a family pastime for tens of thousands of people, complete with field guides and official rules on how many kilos you may take home. And **smučanje** (skiing) is taught in primary school; nearly every Slovenian can ski before they can ride a bike.

The sentence that opens a conversation anywhere: *Lepo vreme, kajne?* (nice weather, isn't it?). *Kajne* at the end of a sentence means "isn't it?" or "right?" and is used exactly like that — a polite question that doesn't demand an answer.

blocks.title: Three comparison sentences to use today
items: *Danes je topleje kot včeraj.* — It's warmer today than yesterday.
*To je najboljša kava v Ljubljani.* — This is the best coffee in Ljubljana.
*Ljubljana je manjša kot Jakarta, ampak lepša.* — Ljubljana is smaller than Jakarta, but more beautiful. (Say this to a Slovenian and watch their reaction.)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right comparative form.
items: To je ____ kava v mestu. (naj + dober)
To je ____ dan v letu. (naj + lep)
